title: Integrals
intro: An integral adds up a quantity that varies, by cutting it into thin pieces. On a graph it is the signed area under the curve.

blocks.text: The question

A car's speedometer reading tells you how fast you are going, and you want to know how far you went. At a constant 20 metres per second for 5 seconds the distance is $20 \times 5 = 100$ metres, which is the area of a rectangle on a graph of speed against time. When the speed varies there is no single rectangle. But over a very short time the speed hardly changes, so each short slice is nearly a rectangle. Add the slices.
Riemann sums

Take $f(x) = x^2$ between $x = 0$ and $x = 2$. Cut the interval into $n$ strips of width $\Delta x = 2/n$, and on each strip stand a rectangle whose height is the value of $f$ at one end. With $n = 4$, using the left end of each strip, the heights are 0, 0.25, 1 and 2.25, so the total is $0.5 \times 3.5 = 1.75$. Using right ends the heights are 0.25, 1, 2.25 and 4, giving $0.5 \times 7.5 = 3.75$.
Because $x^2$ is rising here, left rectangles fall short and right ones overshoot, so the true area lies between 1.75 and 3.75. Using more strips squeezes the two together:

blocks.caption: Sums for x² from 0 to 2. Both head towards 8/3 ≈ 2.6667.

widget.title: Left and right rectangles under x²

blocks.text: The two staircases are the tops of the left and right rectangles, and the legend gives their areas: 1.7500 and 3.7500 at the start. Raise $n$ and both close on the curve. The gap between the two sums is exactly $8/n$.
The definite integral
The definite integral of $f$ from $a$ to $b$ is the limit of such sums as the strips get thinner:

blocks.tex: \int_a^b f(x)\, dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i)\, \Delta x, \qquad \Delta x = \frac{b - a}{n}

blocks.text: Here $x_i$ is any point in the $i$th strip. For a continuous function on a finite interval, every choice leads to the same limit. The sign $\int$ is a stretched S for sum, $dx$ stands for the vanishing width, and $a$ and $b$ are the limits of integration. The result is a number. The letter inside does not matter: $\int_a^b f(t)\, dt$ is the same number.
Signed area

Where $f$ is negative, $f(x_i)\, \Delta x$ is negative, so area below the axis is subtracted. Over a full period, $\int_0^{2\pi} \sin x\, dx = 0$: the hump above and the dip below cancel. If you want the total area regardless of sign, integrate $|f(x)|$, which here gives 4. This cancelling is what Fourier analysis (#/math/fourier-transform) uses to pick one frequency out of a signal.

items: Integrals add over pieces: $\int_a^b f + \int_b^c f = \int_a^c f$.
They are linear: $\int_a^b (\alpha f + \beta g) = \alpha \int_a^b f + \beta \int_a^b g$ for constants $\alpha$, $\beta$.
Swapping the limits changes the sign: $\int_b^a f = -\int_a^b f$.

blocks.text: The fundamental theorem of calculus
Adding up thousands of rectangles is hard work. The shortcut comes from letting the upper end move. Define the area function

How fast does $A$ grow? Moving the end from $x$ to $x + h$ adds a thin strip of width $h$ and height about $f(x)$. So $A(x+h) - A(x) \approx f(x)\, h$, and dividing by $h$ and taking the limit gives $A'(x) = f(x)$, for continuous $f$. The rate at which area builds up is the height of the curve.

A function whose derivative is $f$ is called an antiderivative of $f$. Any two antiderivatives on an interval differ by a constant. So if $F$ is any antiderivative, $A(x) = F(x) + C$, and since $A(a) = 0$ we get $C = -F(a)$. Therefore:

blocks.caption: the fundamental theorem of calculus, with F' = f and f continuous

blocks.text: For $x^2$, an antiderivative is $x^3/3$, because its derivative is $x^2$. So the area from 0 to 2 is $8/3 - 0 = 8/3$, the number the rectangles were creeping towards.
Antiderivatives worth knowing

Each is a derivative rule (#/math/calculus/derivatives) read backwards. For $1/x$ with $x < 0$, the chain rule gives the derivative of $\ln(-x)$ as $\frac{-1}{-x} = \frac{1}{x}$, which is why the table has $\ln |x|$. The constant $C$ records that adding a constant does not change the derivative.

An expression like $\int f(x)\, dx$ with no limits, called an indefinite integral, means the family of all antiderivatives. Not every simple function has an antiderivative you can write with familiar functions: $e^{-x^2}$ does not, and its areas are computed numerically.
Two methods
Substitution: the chain rule backwards

In $\int_0^1 2x\, e^{x^2}\, dx$, put $u = x^2$, so $du = 2x\, dx$. The limits change with the variable: $x$ from 0 to 1 means $u$ from 0 to 1. The integral becomes $\int_0^1 e^u\, du = e - 1 \approx 1.718$.
Integration by parts: the product rule backwards

blocks.tex: \int_a^b u\, v'\, dx = \left[ u v \right]_a^b - \int_a^b u'\, v\, dx

blocks.text: The bracket means the value of $uv$ at $b$ minus its value at $a$. For $\int_0^1 x e^x\, dx$ take $u = x$ and $v' = e^x$, so $u' = 1$ and $v = e^x$. Then $[x e^x]_0^1 - \int_0^1 e^x\, dx = (e - 0) - (e - 1) = 1$.
Improper integrals: running to infinity
The Laplace (#/math/laplace-transform) and Fourier transforms integrate over an infinite range. That is defined as one more limit: integrate up to $b$, then let $b$ grow.
If the limit exists the integral converges, otherwise it diverges. The most useful case is a decaying exponential with $c > 0$:

With $c = 2$ the partial areas are 0.4323 at $b = 1$ and 0.49998 at $b = 5$, closing on one half. An infinitely long region can have a finite area. The same formula holds for complex $c$ whenever its real part is positive, A complex $c$ is written $\sigma + j\omega$, with $j$ the imaginary unit (mathematicians write $i$). A complex-valued function is integrated by integrating its real and imaginary parts separately, and the rule for $e^{kx}$ in the table above still holds for complex $k$. Since $e^{-j\omega b}$ is a point on the unit circle, the size of $e^{-cb}$ is $e^{-\sigma b}$, which still shrinks to 0 as $b$ grows. This is the fact the Laplace transform starts from.

A function going to zero is not enough. $\int_1^b \frac{1}{x}\, dx = \ln b$ grows without bound, so that integral diverges, while $\int_1^b \frac{1}{x^2}\, dx = 1 - \frac{1}{b}$ converges to 1. The second function falls off fast enough and the first does not.
An integral over the whole line, from $-\infty$ to $\infty$, is split at any point, and both halves must converge on their own.
What integrals measure

items: Change from rate: distance from velocity, charge from current, since $Q = \int i(t)\, dt$.
Average value of $f$ on an interval: $\frac{1}{b - a} \int_a^b f(x)\, dx$.
Probability from a density: the chance of landing between $a$ and $b$ is the area under the density there.
Overlap of two signals: Convolution (#/math/convolution) is the integral of a product.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Area under a line
blocks.text: Find $\int_1^3 2x\, dx$ and check it with geometry.
solution: An antiderivative is $x^2$, so the value is $9 - 1 = 8$.
The region is a trapezium with parallel sides 2 and 6 and width 2: area $(2 + 6)/2 \times 2 = 8$.

blocks.title: Signed area
blocks.text: Find $\int_{-1}^{2} x\, dx$.
solution: The triangle below the axis (area 0.5) is subtracted from the one above (area 2).

blocks.title: Average of a sine hump
blocks.text: What is the average of $\sin x$ from 0 to $\pi$?

blocks.title: To infinity
blocks.text: A current $i(t) = 3 e^{-t/4}$ amperes flows from $t = 0$ (in seconds) onwards. How much charge passes in total?

blocks.title: By substitution
blocks.text: Find $\int_0^2 \frac{x}{x^2 + 1}\, dx$.
solution: Put $u = x^2 + 1$, so $du = 2x\, dx$ and $u$ runs from 1 to 5.
